analysis.one_liner: Requires quarterly public reports on Medicare and Medicaid fraud cases and recoveries.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; it was referred to two committees in September 2024 and to a subcommittee in December, a month before the session ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare and Medicaid pay tens of billions of dollars each year, and some of that money is lost to fraud by providers and companies that bill the programs. This bill would require the Department of Health and Human Services' internal watchdog to report to Congress every three months for two years: how many fraud investigations it ran, how many prosecutions and lawsuits it started, how much money was allegedly taken, and how many people or companies were barred from federal health programs. It authorizes no new money and creates no new enforcement power; it would just make existing fraud-fighting work visible to lawmakers every quarter.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who fund Medicare and Medicaid, and the millions of people enrolled in the programs, would benefit indirectly: a regular public accounting of fraud investigations and prosecutions makes it easier for Congress to see whether enforcement is keeping up, and easier to spot providers barred for fraud. Members of Congress on the health committees get a routine data stream to act on.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the HHS Inspector General to report to the four congressional health committees every three months for two years on Medicare and Medicaid fraud investigations, prosecutions, dollar amounts alleged, and program exclusions [S2].
The first report is due three months after enactment, so lawmakers would get a regular, current picture of fraud enforcement rather than occasional ad hoc updates [S2].
The bill is deliberately cheap: it authorizes no additional funds and must be carried out with the Inspector General's existing budget [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the cost would be essentially administrative: the Inspector General's office would compile the reports from records it already keeps, within its existing budget. Providers and companies that defraud Medicare or Medicaid would face greater visibility, since their prosecutions and exclusions would be listed for Congress every quarter.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Inspector General's existing budget; fraudulent billers

drawbacks.text: The bill creates no new enforcement tools, funding, or penalties — it only requires reporting, so it does not itself recover any money; the title's promise to get healthcare money back is aspirational [S2].
It adds a recurring reporting workload to the Inspector General without new funding, and reports to Congress can sit unread if no committee acts on them [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is negligible and the reporting requirement is a reasonable transparency measure, but the benefit is indirect: the bill informs Congress rather than directly stopping fraud or recovering dollars. It would be worthwhile only if the health committees actually used the quarterly reports to strengthen enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It went to two House committees when it was introduced, then to a Health Subcommittee in mid-December, and Congress adjourned before any committee or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Aaron Bean introduced the bill on September 18, 2024, with Reps. Allen and Grothman as original cosponsors; two other members had joined by the end of the Congress [S1][S2][S3].
The Speaker assigned it to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, a dual referral that means either committee could have taken it up [S1].

Neither committee acted; on December 17, 2024, less than three weeks before the session ended, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, where it died with no markup, no vote, and no floor action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much either way — the bill was small. The practical effect is that fraud-enforcement statistics continue to reach Congress only on the watchdog's own schedule, which suits any provider preferring less frequent scrutiny of Medicare and Medicaid fraud prosecutions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; no one moved either way

industries.industry: Medicare and Medicaid providers and billing companies
industries.note: The bill targets fraud by entities billing Medicare and Medicaid; quarterly reporting of prosecutions, alleged dollar amounts, and program exclusions would put more public light on the worst actors. Honest providers would bear no new burden beyond the visibility of enforcement statistics.

The watchdog would gain a mandated recurring audience for its enforcement work but would take on a reporting workload with no new funding. Its interests in more visible enforcement run alongside taxpayers' interests.
